newsitem.title: USA: U.S. aides vow thorough probe of CIA crack charge.
newsitem.headline: U.S. aides vow thorough probe of CIA crack charge.

text.p: Government investigators vowed on Wednesday to get to the bottom of charges that the Central Intelligence Agency may have played a key role in introducing "crack" cocaine to black U.S. inner cities in the 1980s to fund an anti-communist crusade in Nicaragua.

The inspectors general of the CIA and Justice Department testified before the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence that they recently began far-ranging internal investigations that would in effect let the chips fall where they may.

"I would like to assure you and the American public that my office will conduct as thorough a review as possible of all available information and will report what we find candidly and completely," CIA Inspector General Frederick Hitz said in a prepared statement.

The probes were triggered by a three-part series on Aug. 18-20 in the San Jose Mercury News that purported to trace the origins of the U.S. crack epidemic to a pair of Nicaraguan drug traffickers linked to the U.S.-backed Contra rebels.

In defiance of a congressional ban on funding, the CIA under then-President Ronald Reagan helped arm and finance the "contras" against the Marxist Sandinista government that ruled Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990.

Last month, CIA Director John Deutch said in a letter to members of Congress that a preliminary review by his staff had found that the spy agency "neither participated in nor condoned drug trafficking by contra forces." Deutch added that the CIA never had any ties to Danilo Blandon and Norwin Meneses, the two Contra backers said by the Mercury News to have funnelled drug-running profits to the rebels.

The Senate hearing was interrupted repeatedly by people sceptical of the CIA's and Justice Department's ability to investigate themselves, and Committee Chairman Arlen Specter and Vice Chairman Bob Kerrey threatened to clear the room.

Both Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican, and Kerrey, a Nebraska Democrat, termed it critical to get to the bottom of the charges, which they said were contributing to "deep-seated cynicism" about government.
Inspector General Michael Bromwich of the Justice Department said: "The facts and nothing but the facts will drive our investigation."

As the CIA's in-house watchdog for the past five years, Hitz contended he had earned a reputation for independence and objectivity for investigating such scandals as human rights abuses in Guatemala and the case of CIA officer Aldrich Ames, who long eluded detection as a Moscow spy inside the agency.

In many ways, Hitz said, charges of involvement in drug trafficking were "the most politically charged and potentially damaging" of all the alleged wrongdoing he had looked into involving the CIA. "While some may choose not to believe findings that do not correspond to their preconceptions, we will present the unvarnished truth as we find it," he said.
